PD Seminar - Module 6 
his document is a companion document to the PD Seminar – Module 1 that covers Basic PD Theory 
and Detection. Someone in your company has decided that you should use an Iris portable 
instrument or continuous monitoring system to assist in monitoring the condition of your high voltage 
insulation in your motors, generators, switchgear or air-cored transformers, thus you have been asked 
to attend this training seminar. This manual is a textbook used as a reference for the PD Seminar; it is only 
intended to enable the reader to better perform PD testing on motors, generators, switchgear and transformers. 
The manual is not considered a technical presentation of insulation designs or partial discharge theories. 
Hereafter in this manual, 
PDA-IV, TGA-B e and TGA-S will be called Portables; 
HydroGuard, BusGuard and TurboGuard will be called Guards; 
PDA Bantam and TGA Bantam will be called Bantams; 
HydroTrac, BusTrac and PDTrac will be called Tracs; 
and, all test instruments will be called Iris instruments. 
The partial discharge monitoring system described here is to be done with the asset operational and by non-PD 
experts. The software is easy to use and the data easy to interpret thereby enabling you to plan maintenance as 
required. The purpose of this seminar is to provide enough information to do the following: 
• Use PDView 3Ô software to manage data, generate reports 
• Do basic analysis of PD data 
 
Seminar Textbook 
Throughout this textbook, you will see these icons to indicate issues that require your special attention. The 
review questions will be completed during the training seminar. As much as possible, technical terms will be 
explained when they are used; however, in the event that a term is overlooked, you should refer to the glossary 
in the PD Seminar - Module 1. Further information

he PDView 3 software package complements and enhances Iris Power’s Instruments in their ability 
to measure partial discharge activity in motors, turbine generators, hydrogenerators and large turbo 
generators. 
With PDView 3, test results from the testing instrument can be displayed and interpreted through the 
use of various graphical reports. The user does not have to be an expert to produce quality reports, though a 
basic understanding of partial discharge (PD) theory and of the Microsoft Windows environment is assumed. 
Since users of PD technology have different requirements for the functionality embedded in PDView 3, there 
are three different user-interfaces of varying complexity. The levels of user interface are: Simple, Standard and 
Advanced modes. 
 
PDView 3 offers a great deal of flexibility and creativity for those who like to experiment or prefer to use user 
defined customized formats in the Advanced mode. Both the Simple and Standard modes are designed with an 
easy, user-friendly interface that will meet the majority of the customer’s needs. This document only provides 
an overview of the application, for further information consult the PDView User’s Manual. 
 
The development of continuous stator winding monitors, portable rotor winding monitors and monitors for 
other electrical equipment such as transformers and switchgear, as well as the integration of these into local 
plant systems have resulted in increased requirements for a new database design. The Iris Instrument Database 
(IID) design was developed to meet all of these needs. The IID design constitutes a unified database for all 
instruments of Iris Power. The implementation of the IID is in Microsoft® Access1 and requires conversion of 
all Paradox®2-based data previously collected with any of the Iris instruments.

A.1 General Functions 
General functions of PDView 3 may be accessed via the Menu Bar. These options are only available 
when applicable. When a report is not open, the following menus are available; File, Edit, View, Tools, 
Help. When a report is open the following are available; File, Edit, View, Format, Tools, Window, 
Help. 
 
 
Under the File menu the user can Open, Refresh, Backup, Restore and Close a Database. The user can 
also create a New Report, Open, Close, Save and Print an existing report. In addition to these options 
the user can Send the report via email, Export Image to another software application (for example 
Microsoft Excel) or look at the Summary Information for that report. 
 
Under the Edit menu are a number of options for creating, editing and formatting a report. The options 
under View menu allow the user to adjust the user interface window, for example, turning on or off the 
Summary Window. 
 
The Tools menu holds three important options: Database Converter, Filters and Options. Selecting the 
Database Converter will open the converter tool so the user may select the database to convert from 
Paradox® to IID. Selecting Filters will open a screen where the user can define filters for paring down a 
test set from a large database. The Options tool is used to select the User Level, Simple, Standard or 
Advanced mode, as well as select additional application options. 
 
The Format menu provides options for formatting an active graph within the report the user is creating. 
Under the Window menu the user can rearrange the various window components of the general user 
interface.

A.2 User Levels 

Initially, PDView 3 defaults to the Simple user 
interface. This user level provides functionality 
similar to that of the older versions of PDView, 
i.e. easy access to Trend Plots, two-dimensional 
(2D) Pulse Height Analysis plots and three-
dimensional (3D) Pulse Phase Analysis plots. 
This level is for users who use PDView 3 
infrequently and who generally need a tool for 
generating basic test reports, not detailed pulse 
phase analysis. You can change the User level 
through ToolsOptions. 
In the second level, Standard, the user gains 
access to all of the functionality previously 
embedded in AdvanceView. Not only does the 
user have access to Pulse Height and Pulse 
Phase Analysis Reports and Trend Reports, but 
also Standard allows the user access to 
predefined plots for phase-shifted pulse phase 
analysis reports for identification of cross-
coupled partial discharge. This level is for a user who applies interpretational tools such as identification of 
polarity predominance via 2D Pulse Height Analysis plots, identification of classic PD positions via a 3D Pulse 
Phase Analysis Plots and identification of progressive aging via Trend plots. This user is also able to identify 
load or temperature effects. 
The third level, Advanced, allows the user access to functionality which exceeds that of the current 
AdvanceView application. Among other features this includes the definition of new PD counters based on 
fundamental PD counters and the definitions of new graphs and plots. This level is for a user who applies 
advanced interpretation techniques to on-line PD data and performs rudimentary data manipulation tasks.

A.2.1 Simple Mode 
 
Simple Mode functionality allows for: 
 Display of Trend Plots for NQN and Qm for one phase 
 Display of Pulse Height Analysis and Pulse Phase Analysis for one phase 
 Generation of PD Reports 
 Trend Report 
 Pulse Height Analysis and Pulse Phase Analysis Report 
A.2.2 Standard Mode 
 
The aim for the Standard Mode design was to create a user-friendly interface, containing the functionality 
embedded in AdvanceView, while maintaining a simple and intuitive structure. Compared to AdvanceView, 
PDView 3 contains several new features, which not only makes definition of PD graphs easier, but also aids 
interpretation of the acquired data. 
Standard Mode Features: 
 Pre-defined templates allow for a quick definition of phase-shifted Linear Pulse Density Plots for 
identification of phase-to-phase PD sources as well as cross-coupled PD. 
 PD reports may be saved as documents containing not only the report formatting but also the raw PD 
data sets used in the report. Thus, a saved PD report may be opened on a later date and manipulated 
without opening the source database. 
 Direct e-mailing of reports to Iris Power for further analysis. 
 Rudimentary data manipulation including creation of custom PD counters. 
 Export of Raw Data to a .csv file pre-formatted for quick data manipulation in external application 
software. 
 Export of individual graphs and plots to image files or the clipboard for use in documents 
 Export of entire PD reports as image files for use in presentations and documents. 
A.2.3 Advanced Mode 
 
The additional features embedded into Advance Mode are: 
 Display of Advanced Summary Numbers 
 Custom graph types and text control tools 
 Creation of custom PD reports 
 Creation of custom PD Templates 
Compared to Standard Mode, the Template Window for Advanced Mode contains two extra short cut bars: 
Report Tools as well as Custom. Report Tools contains graph objects (graph types and text controls) for 
generation of reports and templates whereas Custom contains custom user-defined templates. 
Furthermore, the content of the Machine and Test Specific Window will change upon selecting Advanced 
Mode displaying the Advanced Summary Numbers; positive and negative mode, mean, standard deviation, 
skew and kurtosis will be displayed.

A.3 Using Simple Mode 
 
Figure 2. DataConverter 
 
If necessary, the first step is to convert a database from Paradox to the new IID format using the 
DataConverter (see Figure 2). Once the user has converted and opened the database, reports can be 
created to view the data in its most useful form. 
 
Please refer to the PDView 3 Help Documentation for information on converting databases. 
 
There are three types of graphs that can be viewed in Simple mode: two-dimensional pulse height 
analysis (PHA) graphs, three-dimensional pulse phase analysis (PPA) graphs and trend plots. Pulse 
height analysis graphs represent the relationship between the pulse magnitude and the pulse repetition 
for both positive and negative polarity. Pulse phase analysis graphs represents the relationship between 
phase angle, pulse repetition rate and pulse magnitude. The trend plots show the magnitude of the PD 
activity across time. When looking at a trend plot a zoom function is available for a closer look at 
activity across a shorter time frame. 
 
To add data to a graph, simply select the desired measurements, right-click and select Update Graph. 
Each graph and report can be viewed in Print Preview mode, and as well formatted either by using the 
right-click menu (when a graph is active – double click the graph) or the options listed under the Edit 
menu. 
A.4 Using Standard Mode 
In Standard mode a new window will appear in the user interface. This is the Templates Window. In 
the Template window there are two choices: Portables & Guards and Tracs & Bantams. When the user 
selects New Report, a screen will appear allowing the user to choose what sort of report template to 
open, and for what type of machine data: Portables & Guards or Tracs & Bantams. 
 
Once a template has been opened, to add data to the report simply select the desired measurements and 
drag onto the graph. In Standard mode graphs have three states: default (no line surrounding the box), 
selected (thin line surrounding the box) and activated (thick line surrounding the box). In order to 
format the graph it must be activated (double click). The user is able to define the graph criteria by 
using Counters & Ranges. Counters & Ranges are available when the graph is activated, right-click and 
select Counters & Ranges. Please see the PDView 3 User’s Manual for more information on how to 
define graph criteria. Also under the right-click menu is Measurements. This tool allows the

A.5 Using Advanced Mode 
In Advanced mode, two more options appear under the Template window. These are Report Tools and 
Custom. Report Tools include Pulse Density Linear Plots, Pulse Phase Analysis Plots, Pulse Density

When the user selects a New Report in Advanced mode, it can be from either a blank report, Portables 
& Guards, Tracs & Bantams, or Custom reports. The user can open the selected report as either a 
document or a template. For purposes of demonstration, select the blank report as a Template. In order 
to add Report Tools to the blank template, select the tool needed and drag and drop it on to the blank 
template. 
 
Adding data and formatting the measurement criteria and the graph criteria have the same purposes as in 
Standard mode. In Advanced mode when the user saves a file, four choices are available: PDView 
document (*.pdv), PDView template (*.tpl), Image file (*.jpg, *.bmp, *.dib, *.wmf, .mfp) and data file 
(.csv).

ou have installed the sensors and collected a lot of data, now what? The collection or interrogation 
of data should be repeated at least every six months for machines rated 6kV and up. If a problem 
develops, then the frequency of collection may need to be increased. Due to the short-time frame 
between detection and failure for motors rated less than 4kV, it is recommended that PD analysis be 
done more frequently on these machines. By using the summary variables (see Module 1), trending of data is 
straightforward and useful. Collection of data at different operating parameters may also help in determining 
the condition of the stator winding. 
B.1 Trend Analysis 
The first step of analysis is to compare the results of the current test with any previous test results. If the unit 
operating parameters – voltage, load, winding temperature and gas pressure – are similar to those of the 
previous test, then a direct comparison can be made between the two test results. For cases where the operating 
parameters are not the same, refer to other sections in this document (Sections B.4.2-B.4.5). In order to 
compare tests it is best to maintain operating conditions within certain ranges, such as: 
Voltage +/- 200V PD increases with voltage, so variances in voltage can 
lead to fluctuations in PD levels 
Load +/- 10% 
Real power +/- 10% 
Reactive power +/- 10% 
If a machine has PD that is mechanically dependent, such 
as loose coils or connections, then it is likely the PD 
levels will change with load. 
Stator 
temperature +/- 5°C Operating temperature affects the volume of internal 
voids, which affects PD magnitudes. 
Hydrogen 
pressure 
+/- 5 psi 
+/- 35kPA 
Gas pressure affects the electrical breakdown stress and 
therefore, levels of PD. 
Humidity Unknown Humidity can affect surface PD, especially PD in the 
endwinding or ring busses 
 
Environmental conditions such as humidity may have a very noticeable impact, especially if the surface 
contamination becomes partly conductive when damp, so it should be recorded from one test to the next. 
It is appreciated that at times it may be very difficult to duplicate test conditions, particularly 
temperatures; however, the emphasis should always be on trying to achieve as uniform conditions as 
possible. This means taking tests when units are hot and the temperature has stabilized. When 
unloading a machine to do a reduced or no load test, it is inevitable the temperature will be in a state of 
transition through the test. In these cases, it is important to quickly conduct the tests to minimize the 
effects of temperature differences. 
 
When a trend line is established for PD tests taken over a period, it will be obvious that most show an up and 
down variation between successive tests. However, as an insulation system ages, there will be a discernible 
overall upward movement of PD with time. Aging is a very slow process and sudden increases are not 
expected in the PD test results. A doubling of PD activity (Qm values twice that of the previous test) every six

Baseline – no trend data available 
Stable – no evidence of changes in stator winding condition (+/- 25%) 
Downward trend new machine – typical for PD on a new winding to decrease during the

Rapid deterioration – rapidly increasing PD and is cause for concern; subsequent tests are

Fluctuations – PD often fluctuates due to variances in ambient and operating conditions, and does

B.2 Comparison to Similar Machines 
As mentioned in Section B.1, data collected from the same machine operating under similar parameters using 
the same test setup are directly comparable and the most useful. It is also possible to roughly compare the 
results of one machine to those of similar machines. Due to the influence of the test arrangement on the results, 
the test setup (sensors and test instrument) must be the same for all comparisons. Based on statistical analysis, 
the type of machine does not appear to have a great impact to PD levels and though insulation types have 
different types of failure mechanisms, in these gross comparisons there does not appear to be much difference 
in the overall levels of PD activity. Load and temperature can also greatly influence test results, but these are 
dependent upon the type and condition of the insulation system, and thus, cannot be used in these gross 
comparisons. The remaining operating variables – voltage and gas coolant – must be similar to compare results 
[Ref. 8 – Module 1]. 
Available as a handout are statistical summaries of the Qm values based on the Iris database that contains over 
43,000 test results [Ref. 11 – Module 1]. Data are separated by sensor, 
gas coolant, and voltage class. All of the data was acquired using an Iris 
test instrument, either a Portable or Guard instrument. Each table shows 
the average, maximum, and the 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th, and 95th percentile 
ranks. The 25th percentile is the Qm magnitude for which 25% of the test 
results are below and are too small to interpret, similarly for 50%, 75%, 
90%, and 95%. Normally, there is concern for a winding if the Qm in a 
machine is higher than the 90th percentile and increasing. 
B.3 PD Characteristics 
B.3.1 Comparison Between Phases 
When the PD levels and patterns are similar among the phases, then uniform deterioration is suspected; 
otherwise, an isolated problem is more likely. Typically, coil looseness, thermal deterioration, contamination, 
and problems with the voltage stress coatings are widespread, or uniform, whereas, improper manufacturing 
and inadequate spacing are often isolated problems. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
B.3.2 Pulse Distribution 
The pulse distribution with respect to the AC phase position in the 3D plots 
can assist in determining the source of any problems in the stator winding. 
Normal pulse distributions are Gaussian, with a standard deviation of 15°, and 
are indicative of spherical shaped voids within the slot section of the core (see 
Figure 5). Narrow band pulses usually originate from PD occurring at sharp 
metallic corners, such as connections. Wide band pulses may indicate multiple 
failure mechanisms or perhaps elongated voids (see Section B.6). PD patterns 
scattered across the ac cycle suggests either contamination, noise, or perhaps a 
combination of several failure mechanisms occurring simultaneously. If the PD 
is evenly distributed across the ac cycle, usually in distinguishable streams, 
often 6 in number, then the source of the pulses is typically from static 
excitation systems and not indicative of a problem with the winding (see Figure 
16). Void shapes are rarely standard and often result in unusual patterns that 
cannot be easily described. One example of unusual patterns is when the PD is 
skewed, non-Gaussian, because of space charge effects within the voids (see

B.4 Classic PD Pulses 
Inspection of the phase resolved plots, especially the Linear Pulse 
Density Plot, reveals the phase angle relationship between the PD 
pulse and the phase-to-ground reference voltage. PD that 
originates within the slot portion of the coil, internal, is centered 
near 45° of the AC cycle for negative pulses and 225° for positive 
pulses. This is the classic position for pulses dependent upon 
phase-to-ground voltage levels of the specific phase being 
measured (see Figure 7). Phase-to-ground voltage stresses occur 
all along coils within the length of the slots in the stator iron. 
Hence, this type of display is indicative of PD occurring in the 
slot and is sometimes referred to as slot-based PD. 
 
 
 
B.4.1 Polarity Predominance 
The polarity of the classic pulses and their predominance tells a 
lot about the relevant failure mechanism as shown in Figure 8. 
Due to space charge effects, a pulse will occur in a specific 
direction based on the proximity of the void to a metallic 
substance. For this reason, it is possible to determine where the 
pulses originate, and therefore, the location of the voids in the 
insulation system. Several failure mechanisms produce voids 
predominantly at a certain location in the insulation. By 
observing the pulse polarity it is often possible to determine 
which failure mechanism is dominant. Note that polarity 
predominance should be based only on the classic PD patterns, 
and in the absence of classic PD, polarity predominance is not 
applicable.

B.4.1.1 Positive Predominance 
 
The Linear Pulse Density plot is inspected to determine whether there is a strong predominance of positive 
pulses of the classic PD, centered near 225° (see Figure 9). Due to pulse behavior, positive predominance 
normally indicates PD originating on the surface of the insulation system, such as slot discharge, endwinding 
tracking, and gradient or semicon coating deterioration. Surface PD happens when a coil does not have 
intimate contact with the core due to shrinkage, improper installation, looseness, or perhaps degradation of the 
voltage stress control coatings. Often the problems associated with surface PD are repairable by common 
maintenance practices such as rewedging, cleaning, dips and bakes, and repairs of the voltage stress coatings. 
 
 
B.4.1.2 Negative Predominance 
 
The Linear Pulse Density Plot is inspected to determine whether or not there is a strong predominance of 
negative pulses of the classic PD, centered near 45° (Figure 10). Due to pulse behavior, negative 
predominance normally indicates PD originating near the conductor surface inside the insulation system. Such 
PD may be the result of voids created due to either improper manufacturing or load cycling that has stressed the 
bonds between the conductor and the first layers of insulating tape. This internal separation of the groundwall 
at the conductor due to load cycling is because of the high conductor temperature and thermal expansion forces 
that cause failure of the bonds between the conductor and the insulation. Eventually, after many years of 
service, even well made windings will start to show signs of distress in this area. Because of the location of the 
voids, that is, near the copper conductors, there are no reliable repair mechanisms for this problem. It may be 
possible to retard the deterioration by altering operating procedures, such as fewer load swings or the addition 
of more sophisticated cooling techniques that restrict the range of the machine operating temperatures. PD near 
the turn insulation in multi-turn coils may lead to winding failure quicker than similar PD in Roebel bars.

If the negative and positive graphs are virtually superimposed on the Pulse Height Analysis plot, then most of 
the PD is probably occurring within the thickness of the groundwall insulation (Figure 11). When the PD 
occurs at the classic positions of 45° and 225° on the 3-D plots, the discharges are phase-to-ground dependent

Such PD is normally the result of thermal deterioration (overheating) of the insulation system that has forced 
the organic bonding material of the insulation to lose its adhesive strength. When this occurs, the insulating 
tapes are no longer held in a consolidated form and the layers begin to separate. PD occurs in the voids thus 
created. In a new insulation system, the presence of excessive PD of this type could be an indication of poor 
impregnation resulting in void inclusions within the insulation build. As with the voids near the copper 
conductors, these voids in the bulk of the insulation are not repairable. Though restoration of the damaged 
insulation is not possible, reductions in the operating temperature of the winding may slow down the 
degradation.

Positive predominance and load dependent PD usually indicates loose coils (positive – with load). Positive predominance 
without load dependence is often a warning of electrical slot discharge (positive – no load). Slot discharge activity usually 
develops in two stages. During the first stage, the semi-conductive armor is still intact, but as the bar or coil vibrates the 
intermittent separation from the grounded core leads to contact sparking. As the semi-conductive armor deteriorates, the 
surface of the coil loses intimate contact with ground, and the second stage of slot discharge – positive, slot-based, surface 
PD – occurs. Load dependent PD without the positive predominance indicates a problem that is also mechanically 
dependent but not within the slot, such as conductor vibration, connections, or core-iron arcing (No positive – with load). 
The absence of load dependence suggests no looseness that is negatively affected by mechanical forces (None). 
B.4.3 Temperature Effect 
Operating temperature can greatly affect the results from a partial discharge test. 
Various materials respond differently to changes in temperature. These changes can be 
subtle for small variances of +/-5°C, or drastic, doubling and tripling, for greater 
discrepancies of +/-20°C. Performing the PD test with the machine at the same load, 
but at different temperatures, i.e. at least +/-20°C may be able to help further identify 
which failure mechanisms are occurring. These are often referred to as “ Cold” and 
“ Hot” tests. 
B.4.3.1 Negative Effect 
The sizes of voids within a stator winding are usually 
inversely proportional to the operating temperature. 
As temperature increases, the copper and groundwall 
bonding material expand closing voids and thus 
decreasing classic PD (see Figure 13). This effect is 
most significant on asphalt and polyester windings, but 
can also be observed on epoxy windings. A large 
negative temperature effect suggests more severe 
internal delamination. Note that RTD temperatures 
taken outside of the groundwall insulation do not 
quickly reflect changes in the temperature of the 
copper conductor or internal insulation. 
B.4.3.2 Positive Effect 
It may be possible that the positive classic PD actually 
increases with temperature (see Figure 14). This 
phenomenon is frequently an indication of deterioration 
of the semicon/grading coating. As the temperature of 
the stator winding increases, the resistance of the 
coatings decreases and results in an increase in surface 
(positive) PD activity. This problem is generally a very 
slow failure mechanism, but often leads to high ozone 
production in air-cooled machines.

B.4.4 Hydrogen Pressure Effect 
Since the occurrence of a partial discharge is greatly affected by the void shape and 
gas pressure within the void, variances in operating hydrogen pressure can lead to 
high fluctuations of the overall PD activity. These changes can be subtle, for small 
variances of +/-2 psi, or drastic, doubling and tripling, for greater discrepancies of 
+/-5psi. Performing the PD test with the machine at the same load, but at different 
operating pressures, i.e. at least +/-10psi, may be able to help identify which failure 
mechanisms are occurring. If the PD decreases with small increases in the hydrogen 
pressure (negative effect), then the sources of PD are most likely within the hydrogen environment. If there is 
no noticeable change in the PD pattern at different hydrogen pressures (none) or a decrease in PD at lower 
pressure (positive effect), then it is likely the PD is from sources external to the hydrogen environment at the 
machine’s terminals. Note this final statement only applies to Bus installs on hydrogen-cooled machines, not 
for SSC applications. 
B.4.5 Humidity Effect 
Perhaps the most influential, yet 
unpredictable, impacts of ambient 
conditions to PD are the effects of 
variances in ambient humidity on air-
cooled machines. Humidity can cause the 
electrical breakdown stress of the air to 
decrease, and therefore cause an increase 
in surface PD. Humidity can affect the 
electrical tracking of surface PD, and 
therefore cause a decrease in PD. Thus, 
in some circumstances, the PD may go 
up, while in others it would go down with 
increases in relative humidity. In some 
circumstances, the humidity effect has 
been known to cause the PD to 
fluctuation by as much as 300%. Since 
each scenario is different, it is extremely 
important the ambient humidity be 
recorded at test time so trends can be 
properly evaluated and decisions are not 
made about upward trends that occur 
because of humidity effects and not 
changes in winding condition. Present 
experience indicates humidity only affects 
surface activity. 
 
B.5 Non-classic Pulses 
Pulses clustered at positions of the phase 
cycle other than 45° and 225° may be 
contingent upon other voltage references, 
such as phase-to-phase voltage, phase-to-
ground voltage from another phase, 
excitation, poor contact sparking or 
surface corona. There may be some 
pulse-shifts at other angles, but these are 
infrequent. Since the PHA plot only 
shows negative pulses occurring between 
-15° and 135° and positive pulses 
between 165° and 315°, a quick way to

determine whether or not the pulses are classic or non-classic is to compare the PHA results to the phase-
resolved results. Pulses on the phase-resolved plots that are not indicated on the PHA plots are indications of 
non-classic PD occurring. 
B.5.1 Interphasal PD 
Several PD sources may be found that are dependent upon phase-to-phase electrical stress. Often the presence 
of these discharge sources can be related to contamination, inadequate spacing, poor contact between the 
semicon and the field-graded area or, as in the case of PD in the groundwall insulation, poorly impregnated 
windings. Although most of the mentioned phenomena give rise to surface discharges, as opposed to 
discharges internal to the insulation, these phenomena may eventually lead to a phase-to-phase or phase-to-
ground failure. It should be mentioned that discharge activity on the ring bus or between phase leads is also 
phase-to-phase dependent discharge activity. 
For voids within the bulk of the insulation, the electrical field distribution controls partial discharge activity. 
Since the fields in the endwinding area are phase-to-phase voltage dependent and the electrical fields in the slot 
area are phase-to-ground voltage, it is often possible to distinguish between discharge activity occurring in the 
slot part and the endwinding part of the winding using phase-resolved analysis. Phase-to-phase voltage 
dependent PD pulses will be +/- 30° phase shifted from the classic positions, or centered at 15°, 75°, 195° and 
255° positions along the representative sine wave. 
By creating an LPD for each phase of a given machine, with the reference phase-to-ground voltage shifted 120° 
between phases based on phase rotation, the discharge activity will be presented in the time domain (see 
Module 1). As shown in Figure 15, there is a source of phase-to-phase PD occurring between high voltage 
components of A-phase (15° and 195°) and B-phase (75° and 255°). This PD is cross-coupled to C-phase 
(315°). 
B.5.2 Cross-coupled PD Activity 
PD pulses are high frequency pulses that may capacitively couple from one phase to another across the 
endwinding or circuit ring. In addition, a coupler connected to one phase may detect pulses radiated from the 
source in another phase. This behavior is called cross coupling and can be detected by observing PD pulses 
shifted +/- 120° from the positions of the source PD. Classic PD cross-coupled from another phase would 
cluster at 345°, 105°, 165° and 285°. Cross-coupled interphasal activity would be +/-30° phase-shifted from 
these positions as shown for C-phase (315°) in Figure 15. Cross-coupled PD is dependent on the geometry of 
the stator winding and does not necessarily indicate a problem with the insulation. Additionally, based on the 
mode of pulse travel, the pulses may invert in polarity. 
 
B.5.3 Excitation Pulses 
PD couplers sometimes detect the high frequency 
thyristor-firings of static excitation systems. These 
pulses are usually of equal pulse repetitions, low 
magnitudes and occur at even phase angles across the 
cycle (Figure 16). These are usually only discernible 
when there is low PD activity on the unit and the 
scale on the PD test instrument is set to its most 
sensitive (lowest range) setting. Such patterns do not 
indicate a problem with the insulation system.

B.5.4 Other Non-classic Pulses 
There are two other combinations where non-classic PD commonly occurs: 0° and 180°, or 90° and 270°. 
When pulses occur at the ac crossovers, or 0° and 180°, they are usually from a source that is affected by 
mechanical vibration, such as a loose or oxidized connection. Pulses that cluster around 90° and 270° are 
usually from some type of open-air arc, or corona, such as along a circuit ring or severely deteriorated interface 
between the grading and semi-conductive stress coatings. Due to the physical attributes of some installations, 
there may be sources of low-magnitude noise-like PD detected by the couplers. When this situation exists, the 
pulses are low in magnitude and normally manifest themselves across the AC cycle. The magnitude of this 
activity is quite low and as the winding ages, PD originating within the winding will reach higher magnitudes 
and be visible beyond this noise-like PD. 
B.6 Multiple Failure Mechanisms 
Complicated 3-D plots may occur if two 
or more failure mechanisms or processes 
are occurring in the winding at the same 
time [Figure 17]. For example, electrical 
tracking and a loose stator winding could 
be simultaneously occurring which both 
positive polarity predominance and non-
classic pulses would indicate. In these 
situations, off-line PD tests, other 
electrical tests and visual inspection may 
be needed to conclusively separate the 
different failure processes. 
 
B.7 Noise 
The TGA-B, TGA Bantam, BusGuard and BusTrac instruments are capable of classifying PD into three 
categories: Unit PD, Bus PD, and System PD. Both the Bus and System PD are considered “ Noise,” as they 
do not originate within the winding. By using the RAW data mode of the PDView software, it is possible to 
distinguish between the two sources of Noise. The PDA-IV, PDA Bantam, HydroGuard and HydroTrac are 
capable of classifying PD into three categories: C1, C2, and Noise. The TGA-S and TurboGuard classifies 
pulses wider than 20ns as Noise, while the PDTrac classifies pulses that are not characteristically PD as noise. 
For this data, by viewing the Noise plot or the Noise category in the RAW data mode, it may be possible to 
ascertain whether there are significant sources of PD occurring outside of the stator winding, perhaps at 
connections, flexible leads, bus insulators/stand-offs, switchgear, transformers, or connection leads.

You can actually see the values of the pulse-count rates collected in the raw data mode. The raw data displays 
the total pulses counted at each of the 3.6° divisions, 100 total, for each sensor and between the sensors (see 
Figure 18). The pulses are also separated by polarity and coupler classification (see table). Pulses that cannot 
be assigned to a specific coupler are classified as O/U/I (over/under/invalid). The RAW pulses are not phase 
shifted nor are they normalized to pulses per second. This is done by the software before the 3-D plot is 
displayed. Please refer to the instrument user’s manual for more information about the pulse categories.
